proposals.name: Introduces a reusable primitive, not a single-use pipeline
proposals.instruction: Score how much of the contribution is a general object -- an operator, representation, kernel, estimator, layer, or framework -- that another researcher could lift out and apply to a problem the authors never mention. 10 = the abstract's central noun is a new general-purpose construct, stated at a level of abstraction above any one task or dataset (e.g. an averaging operator for arbitrary symmetry groups; a new attention form; a kernel family for reconstruction), and its applicability beyond the demonstration is intrinsic rather than asserted. 5 = a method with one clear generalizable idea but presented bound to a single task. 0 = the contribution is an assembly of existing components wired for one application, where removing the application leaves nothing portable behind. Judge the abstraction level of the contribution itself, not how many experiments it reports.
proposals.rationale: R47 (frame averaging as a general recipe for making any backbone invariant/equivariant), R10 (a new higher-dimensional attention primitive), and R27 (Matern kernel family for implicit surfaces) put a portable object on the table with very little apparatus around it, which a criterion bank organized around 'method + dataset + evaluation' completeness will under-reward. R01 and R03 conversely present three-part pipelines (benchmark + identification method + induction method; activity collection + reward model + fine-tuning) that fill every rubric slot but leave no construct usable outside personality induction or proactive assistance.

proposals.name: Explains why, not only reports that
proposals.instruction: Score the degree to which the abstract delivers an explanation -- a stated mechanism, dynamic, or causal account of a phenomenon -- rather than only evidence that an intervention improved a number. 10 = the abstract's payload is understanding: it names what was happening inside the system, why the previous state of affairs held, and what the finding implies for how readers should think about the object (measurements of network state, dynamics of a regime, decomposition of an effect). 5 = a method paper that offers one mechanistic sentence explaining its own gain. 0 = purely operational: intervention applied, metric moved, no account of why, and the reader learns nothing they could carry to a different system.
proposals.rationale: R29 (extensive measurements of the early training phase, with a label-agnostic account), R50 (a minimalist constructed function that explains edge-of-stability convergence), R59 (stepwise deconstruction showing which diffusion components actually matter), and R22 (two-domain hypothesis explaining why batch norm hurts robust training) are explanation-first with modest headline numbers. R44 and R54 are the opposite shape -- component added, AP or benchmark score up -- and a bank that credits 'clear empirical gains' scores them well while the explanatory papers score thin.

proposals.name: Contribution by subtraction or simplification
proposals.instruction: Score whether the work advances by removing, fixing, or simplifying machinery while preserving capability, as opposed to adding stages. 10 = the paper shows a widely used component is unnecessary, replaces a complex procedure with a markedly simpler or cheaper one, or reduces a multi-stage pipeline to fewer stages, and is explicit that the simpler version matches or nearly matches what it replaces. 5 = a method of ordinary complexity with a genuine efficiency argument. 0 = the contribution is strictly additive -- new modules, extra training phases, extra preference categories, extra generation steps -- with no accounting of what could have been dropped.
proposals.rationale: R26 (the last weight layer can be fixed entirely, with memory and speed benefits), R59 (transforming a diffusion model back into a classical denoising autoencoder), and R27 (easier to implement, faster to compute, five times shorter training) all take value away from the system and still deliver. Rubric banks reward described machinery, so additive designs such as R13 (five preference aspects plus a new optimization objective) and R16 (motif vocabulary, focal selection, attachment, cheminformatics, refinement) accumulate credit for each added part, while subtractive papers present less surface to score.

proposals.name: Enumerated contribution bundle masking thin individual parts
proposals.instruction: Score inversely to contribution-count inflation: how much the abstract relies on enumerating several separately-announced contributions whose individual weight is small, rather than pursuing one idea to depth. 10 = one central claim developed all the way through, with any secondary items clearly subordinate to it. 5 = two genuinely coupled contributions. 0 = the abstract announces 'three major technical contributions' or a First/Second/Third list in which the items are a dataset, a routine application of an existing technique to that dataset, and a simple manipulation, each of which would be unremarkable alone and none of which is developed beyond a sentence.
proposals.rationale: R01 explicitly advertises 'three major technical contributions' and R03 chains collection, annotation, reward model, pipeline and fine-tuning; R13 similarly enumerates five preference categories plus a framework. Each bundle presents many separately scorable items to a criterion bank, inflating a completeness-shaped aggregate. R10 and R28 make a single claim with no enumeration at all and would score near-zero on any per-item counting, despite the claim being sharp.

proposals.name: Headline numbers anchored to an interpretable yardstick
proposals.instruction: Score whether the quantitative claims are anchored so a reader can tell what they mean: named datasets or benchmarks, a named baseline that is a fair comparator, absolute units where units exist, and a scale at which the measurement was taken. 10 = numbers are given against explicitly named comparators on recognized settings, in units that carry meaning (perplexity gap, nanoseconds of error, percent against three named prior methods), so the reader can independently size the advance. 5 = credible numbers with partially specified comparators. 0 = large arena-specific percentages or speedup multipliers whose baseline, budget, or denominator is unstated, so the figure is impressive-looking but unsizable from the text.
proposals.rationale: R14 (within 0.4 PPL on OpenWebText, 1.0 PPL better hybrid, stated parameter counts) and R11 (116.4% over MOPO, 23.2% over MOReL, 23.7% over COMBO, 11 of 18 datasets) give sizable, checkable magnitudes; R06 reports absolute physical error (<0.33ns). By contrast R02's 92.7% versus 28.5% attack success, R08's 6.94x and 2.3x speedups, and R09's 43% mean-error reduction are large round figures whose comparators or budgets are only partly specified -- exactly the shape a 'reports quantitative improvements' criterion rewards without discounting.

proposals.name: Centrality and load-bearing scope of the studied object
proposals.instruction: Score how load-bearing for the field the object of study is: how many other researchers' work depends on the artifact, phenomenon, or question being examined. 10 = the abstract studies something structurally central -- the generalization-error/scale relationship, the expressivity gap between two dominant architecture families, symmetry handling for whole model classes -- so the result propagates to many downstream lines regardless of the specific numbers. 5 = an active but bounded subarea. 0 = the object is a single niche architecture, one proprietary model's idiosyncratic behavior, or a narrowly scoped task setting, such that the finding is unlikely to constrain anyone working outside it.
proposals.rationale: R21 (functional form of generalization error across model and data scales) and R14 (why state space models trail attention in language modeling) study things everything else rests on. R09 improves a single largely superseded memory architecture, R32 tests one model's picture-word interference, and R56 addresses VAE recommender interest modeling; all three are competently executed and will satisfy criteria about rigor and clarity, but the object itself carries little weight, and a criterion bank scoring execution rather than stakes cannot see that difference.

proposals.name: Names a falsifiable hypothesis and follows it through
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract states a specific, falsifiable hypothesis about why the world behaves as it does and then derives an intervention or test from it. 10 = a named hypothesis appears in the text, is used to predict a nonobvious consequence, and the consequence is checked -- the reasoning chain hypothesis -> prediction -> intervention is visible in the abstract. 5 = an informal intuition motivates the design, without a stated prediction. 0 = the abstract proposes a design and reports that it worked, with motivation given only as 'existing methods struggle' and no proposition that could have turned out false.
proposals.rationale: R22 names the two-domain hypothesis, uses it to predict that separate normalization statistics will help, and confirms it; R36 posits that generator nonlinearity induces a stochastic Riemannian metric and derives improved interpolation and a variance fix; R43 builds a definition of label uncertainty and predicts error regions will concentrate there. R05 and R40 identify a deficiency and propose machinery against it with no proposition at risk, yet present all the surface features -- problem, gap, method, gains -- that a rubric bank checks for.

proposals.name: Result contradicts a stated prevailing belief
proposals.instruction: Score how strongly the finding cuts against what the abstract itself identifies as standard practice or received wisdom, with the belief named so the contradiction is legible. 10 = the abstract states what the field assumes and then shows the assumption is wrong or unnecessary in a way that would change practice (a standard component turns out to be droppable; removing training data improves a metric; a widely used consensus condition fails). 5 = a mildly surprising direction with a named prior expectation. 0 = the finding runs in the expected direction -- more supervision, more capacity, or an added module improves the target metric -- with no belief put at risk.
proposals.rationale: R26 (the trained classifier layer is nearly worthless) and R22 (removing clean images from adversarial training raises robustness by 18.3%) both invert standard practice explicitly, and R59 concludes most modern diffusion components are nonessential. R44 (distillation with attention guidance improves detection AP) and R24 (a geometry-motivated regularizer beats prior FSCIL numbers) advance in the anticipated direction; both are well-formed abstracts that a completeness-oriented bank scores highly, while surprise -- which experts weigh heavily -- is not a completeness property.

proposals.name: Reports parity and limits alongside wins
proposals.instruction: Score the calibration of the empirical reporting: does the abstract state where the method ties, where it falls short, or under which conditions the advantage holds, rather than presenting a uniformly positive picture? 10 = the text volunteers the boundary -- ties on the remaining datasets, near-parity in a specified regime, a remaining gap to a stronger reference, an advantage that holds only under a named condition. 5 = mostly positive with one qualified statement. 0 = every reported comparison is a win, superiority is claimed across all settings, and no regime is identified where the method is merely comparable or worse.
proposals.rationale: R11 states state of the art on 11 of 18 datasets and 'on par on the remaining'; R27 says 'almost on par with state-of-the-art in the noise-free case'; R14 concedes coming 'within 0.4 PPL' before reporting where it wins. R44, R31 and R24 report only favorable comparisons. Volunteered limits are informative to an expert but read as missing strength to a bank that scores demonstrated improvement, so calibrated abstracts are penalized exactly where a careful reader trusts them more.

proposals.name: Scope claims calibrated; no promissory boilerplate
proposals.instruction: Score the match between the size of the claim and the evidence the abstract itself describes, penalizing forward-looking filler. 10 = the framing is exactly as large as what was shown, including honest 'towards'/'first attempt'/'we make progress on' framing where the work is genuinely partial, and the closing sentence states a result rather than a hope. 0 = the abstract closes on promissory language -- paves the way, highlights the potential, establishes a new paradigm for future research, unlocks future advancements -- that asserts significance the described evidence does not reach. Score the calibration, not the modesty: a strong, fully supported claim stated plainly also earns 10.
proposals.rationale: R06 ('we work towards a neural surrogate'), R38 ('makes the first attempt'), and R14 ('promising initial results') scope themselves precisely to what they establish. R03 ('paving the way for future advancements'), R05 ('paves the way for more efficient and scalable integration'), and R40 ('provide a new paradigm for future research') close on unearned significance claims; criteria that reward a stated impact or significance statement credit that language rather than discounting it.

proposals.name: Artifact-scale counts substituting for insight
proposals.instruction: Score inversely to reliance on size-of-artifact statistics as the abstract's main quantitative content. 10 = whatever resource was built is described by what it enables one to learn or discriminate, and the reported quantities are findings. 5 = scale figures are reported but a substantive finding carries the abstract. 0 = the quantitative content is almost entirely counts of the authors' own construction -- number of questions, subcategories, events, modalities, models evaluated, memory entries -- with the actual finding compressed into a vague clause such as 'revealing some limitations' or 'highlighting the potential'.
proposals.rationale: R37 leads with 18K questions, 26 subcategories, five modalities and 22 plus 6 models evaluated, closing on 'revealing some limitations'; R03 foregrounds 6,790 events; R60 foregrounds a 150-million-mention memory. Counts are trivially verifiable and read as concrete evidence to a criterion judge, so this shape scores well on rubrics about empirical scale and comprehensiveness while telling an expert little about what was learned. Contrast R28 and R50, which report no artifact scale at all and are pure claim.

proposals.name: Gain not purchased by a stronger teacher, annotator, or compute
proposals.instruction: Score whether the reported advance comes from the idea rather than from importing a more capable external source of supervision or more resources. 10 = the improvement is attributable to the mechanism itself and the abstract makes the cost side explicit (little additional computational cost, fewer parameters, no extra training, shorter training time, no external storage). 5 = ordinary supervision, cost unaddressed. 0 = the pipeline's quality visibly derives from a frontier model generating the training data, from paid human annotation of the training signal, or from distilling a larger model, and the abstract does not separate the contribution of that external source from the contribution of the proposed design.
proposals.rationale: R13 (prompting GPT-4/4o to generate the preference data), R03 (human annotators labeling predictions to train the reward model), and R40 (prompting a strong LLM to refine error actions) all put the decisive quality source outside the method, yet these read as thorough, well-resourced pipelines to a rubric. R26 (fewer parameters, faster inference), R27 (five times shorter training), and R23 ('relatively little additional computational cost') instead price their contribution honestly, and cost-accounting is a property most criterion banks do not score.

proposals.name: Contribution density versus generic background throat-clearing
proposals.instruction: Score the fraction of the abstract that carries specific technical content rather than replaceable framing. 10 = nearly every sentence states something particular to this work -- a definition, a construction, a mechanism, a measured consequence -- with at most one orienting sentence. 5 = a conventional two-to-three sentence background windup followed by substantive content. 0 = a third or more of the text is field-generic preamble ('large language models have become increasingly proficient', 'despite significant advancements', 'have proved their ability to perform complex tasks like humans') that could be pasted unchanged into hundreds of other abstracts, with the actual contribution compressed into the remainder.
proposals.rationale: R01, R05, R53 and R40 all open with interchangeable LLM-progress preamble before reaching their specifics, and that preamble supplies the motivation and significance sentences a rubric bank looks for, so it is rewarded rather than discounted. R10, R48, R34 and R28 begin essentially at the contribution and sustain technical content per sentence; they read as dense to a reader but offer fewer of the discrete framing elements a checklist enumerates.

proposals.name: Defines a precise formal object or measurable quantity
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract introduces a sharply defined object -- a ratio, bound, divergence, complexity rate, definition, or estimand -- precise enough that a third party could compute it, prove something about it, or disagree with the definition. 10 = the definition is stated in the abstract, the conditions under which it is meaningful are indicated, and results are expressed in its terms (a defined cost ratio, sandwich bounds on a specified function, iteration complexity in epsilon, a definition of an uncertainty quantity). 5 = a quantity is used but not defined. 0 = the central concept remains informal throughout (a capability, a desirable behavior, a quality) with no operational definition that would let another group reproduce the measurement.
proposals.rationale: R28 defines the cost of overfitting explicitly as a ratio of test errors and states the agnostic regime in which it is considered; R38 targets the rate-distortion function with two-sided empirical bounds; R34 states iteration complexities; R43 builds on a novel definition of label uncertainty. R03 (proactiveness) and R01 (personality trait induction) keep their central construct informal, delegating definition to a benchmark they built, which nonetheless reads as fully operationalized to a rubric that checks whether the task is defined and evaluated.

proposals.name: Cross-domain transplant with the real obstacle named and solved
proposals.instruction: Score whether an idea imported from another area is adapted against a specific, stated obstacle that made the naive import fail. 10 = the abstract names the source idea, names the concrete reason it does not transfer directly (textures live inside network parameters; wireless signals are a superposition of paths rather than a volumetric integral; weight perturbations destroy accuracy), and describes the specific modification that resolves it. 5 = an import with generic adaptation described at a high level. 0 = a currently popular component is applied to a new target and the novelty is the pairing itself, with no obstacle identified and no adaptation beyond retargeting the inputs and outputs.
proposals.rationale: R06 rederives the volumetric-rendering idea as a superposition of ray-surface path evaluations because the wireless signal is not an image; R12 must add a weight-smoothness prior and distillation because naive coordinate-network fitting of weights loses accuracy; R23 states precisely what standard message passing cannot represent before adding Cartesian multipoles; R25 generalizes flow matching because existing maps cannot express the needed transport. R02 and R35 pair a strong existing generator with a new target, which produces a complete-looking method section for a rubric while the adaptation burden is comparatively light.

proposals.name: Abstract bulk: length plus enumerated contribution expansiveness
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for HOW MUCH text and explicit enumeration the abstract contains, ignoring what it says. Measure bulk only: approximate word count, number of sentences, and the number of separately labelled or enumerated items (for example 'First, ... Second, ... Third, ...', bulleted lines, bolded aspect names, numbered contributions). 0 = very short and unenumerated (roughly under 80 words, no list structure); 5 = mid-length (roughly 150-200 words) with at most one enumerated series; 10 = very long (300+ words) with several enumerated or labelled sub-claims. You must NOT judge whether the length or the enumeration is appropriate, well used, or a sign of a good paper, and you must not treat brevity as either a virtue or a defect; report only how much bulk and enumeration are present.
proposals.rationale: Bulk is mechanically available to any criterion-counting aggregator: a longer, enumerated abstract offers more surfaces on which a fixed criterion can fire, whatever the merit underneath. In this slice the extremes line up with bulk: R54 is two sentences and R14 is four, both sitting in the dense-high/card-low half, while R05 (five bolded preference aspects), R52 (three bulleted results) and R32 ('three major technical contributions') are long and heavily enumerated and sit in the card-high half. Word count is not research quality: R08 and R39 state substantive results compactly, and R47's length comes from having two loosely related observations rather than from having more to show.

proposals.name: Density of numeric performance claims and superlative comparisons
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the abstract packs explicit quantitative result claims and comparative superlatives into its text. Count: numerals attached to results (percentages, accuracy or AP or PPL values, 'x' speedup factors, counts of benchmarks or datasets beaten) and comparison phrases such as 'outperforms state-of-the-art', 'significantly outperforms', 'by a large margin', 'achieves the best'. 0 = no result numerals and no comparative superlatives; 5 = one or two numeric results, or one superlative claim; 10 = many numeric deltas plus repeated superlative comparison language. You must NOT verify, weigh, or judge whether the numbers are impressive, correct, or well earned, and must NOT treat their absence as a flaw; report only how much of this reporting style is present.
proposals.rationale: Numeric-superiority packaging concentrates in the card-high half of the slice: R10 (92.7 percent versus 28.5 percent, plus 49.5 percent black-box), R29 (43.9 AP, 4.1 higher than baseline), R41 (116.4 percent, 23.2 percent, 23.7 percent, 11 of 18 datasets) and R56 (6.94x and 2.3x). The dense-high half often has nothing numeric to state: R39, R08, R26 and R54 report qualitatively, and R44 and R22 are theory papers where a percentage would be meaningless. The channel therefore tracks which genre the paper belongs to and how its community writes results, not whether the work is sound; a theory paper cannot earn the tick and an incremental benchmark paper earns it automatically.
proposals.upstream_parent: subfield and genre reporting convention (empirical-benchmark paper versus theory or analysis paper)

proposals.name: Topic-era vocabulary: current-wave terminology density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much of the abstract's technical vocabulary belongs to the most recent wave of machine-learning terminology, versus earlier-era or era-neutral vocabulary. Recent-wave markers include: 'large language model' or 'LLM', 'agent', 'multimodal', 'foundation model', 'benchmark suite', 'alignment', 'preference optimization', 'in-context', 'prompt', 'diffusion', 'reward model'. Earlier-era or era-neutral markers include: GAN, VAE, LSTM, BERT probing, batch normalization, kernel methods, belief propagation, Bloom filters, meta-RL, purely mathematical vocabulary. 0 = vocabulary entirely earlier-era or era-neutral; 5 = a genuine mixture; 10 = saturated with the newest wave's terms. You must NOT judge whether the topic is important, timely, fashionable, or derivative; report only the share of recent-wave vocabulary.
proposals.rationale: The two halves of the slice differ in era, not only in content. The card-high half is thick with recent-wave vocabulary: R02 (agent tuning and generalization), R60 (proactive LLM agents, reward model), R32 (personality-trait neurons in LLMs), R27 (large multimodal models, benchmark), R49 (self-updatable LLMs). The dense-high half holds many earlier-era or era-neutral entries: R17 (fixing the last weight layer), R54 (2-simplicial Transformer), R44 (kernel ridge regression), R14 (Bloom filters), R30 (early-phase training). When a paper was written is not a property of its research quality, but a criterion bank authored now will find more of its own named concepts in recent-vocabulary text, giving a pure calendar effect that looks like a quality signal.
proposals.upstream_parent: the submission cycle and calendar year in which the item was written, and the hype topic prevailing then

proposals.name: Artifact-availability boilerplate: code, data, project-page announcements
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT of explicit release and availability announcements in the abstract: a code URL, a GitHub or project-page or website link, phrases such as 'code is available', 'our data and code will be available', 'code has been released', or the naming of released checkpoints, benchmarks, annotations or datasets as deliverables. 0 = no availability statement of any kind; 3 = a bare promise of future release with no link; 6 = one concrete link or one clearly named released artifact; 10 = several artifacts announced together (for example code plus data plus model weights plus a project page). You must NOT assess whether releasing is good practice, whether the link looks credible or maintained, or whether the artifact is valuable; count only how prominently availability is announced.
proposals.rationale: Availability sentences cluster in the card-high half of this slice: R01, R05, R10, R33, R43, R45, R48 and R56 all close with a link or an explicit promise, while several dense-high entries make no such announcement at all (R54, R44, R14, R15, R34, R57). A judge working from a fixed criterion bank can tick a reproducibility or openness item off that one sentence without any of the underlying artifact being visible, and the sentence is produced by group practice, engineering capacity and institutional permission rather than by the research itself. Tagged mixed because the same practice plausibly co-occurs with genuinely more careful and checkable work.
proposals.upstream_parent: the producing group's release practice and its compliance with venue and reproducibility norms (engineering support, legal clearance, institutional habit)

proposals.name: Assembly artefacts: unrendered markup, hyphenation breaks, duplicated fragments
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the amount of mechanical text damage and unrendered markup visible in the abstract. Count: line-break hyphenation left inside words (for example 'auto- matic', 'uncer- tainty', 'sur- rounding', 'rigor- ous'); LaTeX or markdown source that has not rendered (backslash-prefixed macros such as textit, texttt, url, epsilon, stray braces, doubled asterisk emphasis markers); malformed, doubled or truncated URLs; duplicated or dangling clause fragments; erratic spacing or stray line breaks mid-sentence. 0 = clean, fully rendered prose; 5 = a couple of hyphenation breaks or one raw macro; 10 = pervasive markup leakage together with visible duplication or truncation. You must NOT judge whether the authors were careless, whether the writing is good, or whether the damage reflects on the science; count only the visible mechanical artefacts.
proposals.rationale: The damage is real and text-visible in this slice: R23 ends with a duplicated corrupted fragment ('...hyper-parameter sensitivity of DRL.ment, mitigating the inefficient exploration...'), R21 carries a broken markdown link ('GEnBP}{github.com/danmackinlay/GEnBP'), R06, R58 and R49 carry PDF-style hyphenation breaks across line ends, and R04 and R10 leave textit, texttt and url macros unrendered. None of this is produced by the research; it is produced by how the text was moved from a PDF or LaTeX source into a submission form, and a text-only scorer can key on it directly. Tagged mixed because the deadline pressure that produces sloppy pasting could plausibly also affect the work itself.
proposals.upstream_parent: the submission and assembly pipeline, and the time pressure under which the final abstract text was pasted into the form

proposals.name: Motivational preamble versus context-assuming terse opening
proposals.instruction: Read only the first two or three sentences of the abstract. Score 0-10 for how much general-audience motivational scene-setting they contain before the paper's own problem or object is named. Preamble markers include: 'With the rapid development of ...', 'X have shown remarkable abilities ...', 'X has garnered widespread attention', 'A fundamental question in ... is', broad statements about how important or promising the field is. 0 = the abstract opens directly on its own technical object, method or result, assuming the reader already knows why it matters; 5 = one framing sentence and then straight to the paper's problem; 10 = several sentences of field-level motivation before the contribution is named. You must NOT judge whether motivating the reader is good or bad writing, and must NOT prefer either style; report only how much preamble is present.
proposals.rationale: The postures separate cleanly in the slice. R27 ('With the rapid development of AI-generated content, the future internet may be inundated ...'), R60 ('Agents powered by large language models have shown remarkable abilities ...') and R02 spend their opening sentences on field-level motivation and sit in the card-high half; R14, R17, R22, R44 and R54 name their own object in the first clause and sit in the dense-high half. How much context an author assumes is a fingerprint of practice in the format and of expected readership, not of research merit, and a criterion asking whether the motivation is clearly established rewards the preamble mechanically. Tagged mixed because practised authors may also do better work.
proposals.upstream_parent: the author's seniority and practice in writing for this venue, i.e. how much shared context they assume their reader already has

proposals.name: Signalled scale of compute, data, and evaluation breadth
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the abstract advertises the SIZE of the resources behind it: parameter counts, corpus or dataset sizes, number of models or baselines evaluated, number of benchmarks or environments used, quantity of human annotation collected, scale of training runs. 0 = no scale of any kind stated; 5 = one dataset or benchmark named at modest scale; 10 = several explicit large magnitudes, for example hundreds of millions of items, dozens of models compared, or many benchmark suites at once. You must NOT judge whether the scale is appropriate, necessary, sufficient, or impressive, and must NOT treat small scale as a weakness; count only how much scale is stated in the text.
proposals.rationale: Advertised scale is a direct textual fingerprint of budget, which is very unevenly distributed across submitters. R27 states 18K curated questions across 26 subcategories and 22 open-source plus 6 closed-source models evaluated; R25 states a memory of 150 million Wikipedia mentions; R60 states 6,790 annotated events with human labellers; R37 reports scaling to 2.7B parameters on the Pile; R13 reports a Mechanical Turk human evaluation and a google-research release path. A criterion bank containing items about thorough evaluation or dataset ambition will fire on budget rather than on insight, and R08, R50 and R54 can never earn those ticks. Tagged mixed because budget does buy some genuine thoroughness.
proposals.upstream_parent: the producing group's compute budget, funding and headcount

proposals.name: Inline citation and named-prior-system lineage density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the abstract explicitly situates itself inside a named lineage. Count: parenthetical author-year citations placed inside the abstract text itself; prior methods, systems or phenomena referred to by proper name and attributed to specific prior work; 'building on', 'following', 'in the spirit of', 'cf.' constructions pointing at particular papers. 0 = no citations and no named prior systems; 5 = two or three named prior systems but no author-year citations; 10 = several author-year citations together with multiple named prior systems. You must NOT judge whether the citing is appropriate, whether the cited lineage is prestigious, or whether the related work is well chosen; report only the density of explicit lineage references.
proposals.rationale: R30 names Frankle et al. 2019, Gur-Ari et al. 2018 and Achille et al. 2019 inside the abstract; R52 names Ioffe and Szegedy, Santurkar et al. and Arora et al.; R59 names Gibson 2017, Blahut 1972, Arimoto 1972 and Balle et al. 2021; R44 adds an explicit 'cf. Mallinar et al. 2022'; R41 names MOPO, MOReL and COMBO as the frame of reference. Writing an abstract as an insider message addressed to a specific lineage is a social positioning habit that leaves a heavy textual trace, and criteria about situating the contribution or engaging the literature will reward it independently of whether the contribution is sound. Tagged mixed because well-embedded authors often do know the literature better.
proposals.upstream_parent: the author's embeddedness in a subfield's citation and social network (who they read, work alongside, and expect to be read by)

proposals.name: Non-idiomatic phrasing and formulaic English collocations
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT of non-idiomatic or formulaic English in the abstract. Markers include: subject-verb or article disagreement; calque-like collocations ('has been a challenging problem as', 'would inevitably cause', 'stuck in the same mistake for a long while', 'in a wide variety of'); stock intensifier templates ('extensive experiments validate the efficacy', 'achieve excellent improvements', 'demonstrate the versatility of our approach'); awkward preposition, tense or determiner choices. 0 = uniformly idiomatic native-standard prose; 5 = a few formulaic or slightly off collocations; 10 = pervasive non-idiomatic construction and stock templating throughout. This is explicitly NOT a judgement of clarity, of the correctness of the science, or of writing quality, and non-idiomatic English must NOT be treated as a defect or a signal of weaker work; report only how much of this surface pattern is present.
proposals.rationale: R01 ('has been a challenging problem as only a few training samples are accessible', 'would inevitably cause a misalignment'), R32 ('Extensive experiments validates the efficacy', with the number disagreement intact), R02 ('frequently stuck in the same mistake for a long while') and R29 ('achieve excellent AP improvements') all carry these markers and all sit in the card-high half of the slice, while R42, R30 and R39 read as fluent native-register prose. The conjectured parent - author language background - cannot be a legitimate ingredient of research quality, so this is a pure nuisance rather than a mixed one; it is nevertheless strongly text-visible and therefore trivially learnable by any text-only scorer, which is exactly why it must be declared and discounted.
proposals.upstream_parent: the authors' first language and the regional writing-school conventions in which they were trained

proposals.name: Late-arrival corrective riff versus first-pass entry framing
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the abstract reads as a late arrival into an already crowded conversation rather than as a first pass at a freshly opened problem. Late-arrival markers include: interrogating, deflating or dissecting an established consensus or a popular method ('Is X really a silver bullet?', 'Is X a free lunch?', 'an open secret in contemporary machine learning', 'this consensus is challenged', 'deconstructing', 'revisiting', 'we argue that current methods undermine ...'); defining the contribution mainly against a named family of existing approaches; cataloguing what many prior works already tried and where they fell short. 0 = none of these; the text reads as an early entry that opens a problem or states that the issue is unexplored ('we make the first attempt', 'this issue still remains unexplored', 'we introduce the notion of'). 5 = the paper positions against prior work but contests no established view. 10 = the entire framing is a corrective or deflationary riff on a saturated line of work. You must NOT judge which posture is better, more novel, more courageous or more valuable, and must NOT treat either end as stronger research; report only how many late-arrival markers the text carries.
proposals.rationale: Position in the stream is unobservable, but the rhetorical posture it induces is fully visible here. Late-arrival framings: R04 ('Is Adversarial Training Really a Silver Bullet ...?', explicitly overturning 'a consensus'), R40 ('Is Factuality Enhancement a Free Lunch ...?'), R42 ('An open secret in contemporary machine learning ...') and R39 ('Deconstructing Denoising Diffusion Models'). First-pass framings: R59 ('makes the first attempt at an algorithm for sandwiching the R-D function'), R05 ('this issue still remains unexplored'), R21 and R11 ('We introduce ...' on ground claimed as new). The posture is a function of when the writer arrived relative to everyone else working the same prompt, not of how good the work is, and it is precisely what criteria about novelty, critical insight or gap identification will latch onto - so it must be a declared nuisance rather than a bank item. Tagged mixed because a late entrant who has watched the obvious takes get taken may also genuinely have more to say.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream - how mature and crowded the topic already was when this item was written and submitted

proposals.name: Mechanistic explanation of why, not just what
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on how much the abstract explains the underlying causal mechanism or reason WHY an observed phenomenon or result occurs, rather than merely stating what was done and what improved. A 10: the abstract states a specific causal hypothesis or mechanism (e.g., a distributional mismatch, an uncertainty gap) and explains how it produces the observed effect. A 0: the abstract lists a technique and a resulting number/improvement with no explanation of why it works.
proposals.rationale: R01 builds and tests a 'two-domain hypothesis' to explain why batch normalization hurts adversarial robustness, and R48 introduces label uncertainty specifically to explain why concentration-of-measure fails to capture intrinsic robustness -- both dense_high_card_low. By contrast R33 (dense_low_card_high) states two engineering fixes mapped to two observed problems but does not develop a deeper causal account.

proposals.name: Explicit surprise / counterintuitive-result signaling
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the abstract explicitly flags a result as surprising, unexpected, or counter to prior belief (e.g., 'intriguing', 'unexpected observation', 'remarkably', or an explicit statement that an assumption turned out false). A 10: the abstract's central claim is framed as overturning an expectation. A 0: the abstract presents its findings as a routine, expected improvement with no framing of surprise.
proposals.rationale: R01 opens by naming 'Intriguing Properties' and an 'unexpected observation', and R34 highlights that a classifier 'can be fixed... with little or no loss of accuracy' against the implicit expectation that it must be learned -- both dense_high_card_low. Numbers-driven abstracts like R03 and R10 present gains as expected payoffs of added engineering, without any surprise framing.

proposals.name: Single unifying idea vs. itemized component checklist
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the abstract is organized around one coherent conceptual idea that drives the whole paper (10) versus a list of several distinctly-named sub-contributions/components introduced one after another with little explanation of how they cohere into one idea (0).
proposals.rationale: R60 and R31 are each driven by a single generalizable idea (a kernel family; a frame-averaging operator) that explains every downstream result -- both dense_high_card_low. R11 ('three major technical contributions': a benchmark, a neuron-identification method, an induction method) and R10 (three separately numbered fixes) read as itemized checklists -- both dense_low_card_high.

proposals.name: Formal guarantee or theoretical proof present
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on the presence of a stated formal/mathematical guarantee (a theorem, complexity bound, convergence proof, or similar) in the abstract. A 10: the abstract states a specific proven guarantee or bound. A 0: the abstract offers no formal claim, only empirical/engineering description.
proposals.rationale: R31 proves its models have 'maximal expressive power in a broad setting' and R14 states a precise iteration-complexity bound -- both dense_high_card_low. R03 and R32 describe entirely empirical engineering pipelines with no formal guarantee -- both dense_low_card_high.

proposals.name: Cross-domain conceptual transfer
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the abstract explicitly imports a concept or technique from a distant field/application area into a new one, naming the source analogy. A 10: the abstract explicitly draws an analogy to a different domain's method and adapts it. A 0: the work stays entirely within its home domain's standard toolkit with no cross-domain framing.
proposals.rationale: R06 explicitly transplants the NeRF idea from vision into wireless channel modeling, and R21 explicitly extends the 2D Segment-Anything idea into the 3D point-cloud domain -- both dense_high_card_low. R33's object-detection distillation stays within the established knowledge-distillation toolkit with no such transfer -- dense_low_card_high.

proposals.name: Names the specific flaw in a prior assumption
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the abstract identifies a SPECIFIC assumption or design choice in prior work and explains precisely why it is wrong or incomplete, rather than a generic 'existing methods underperform'. A 10: names the exact assumption and the mechanism by which it fails. A 0: only asserts prior methods are worse/insufficient without diagnosing why.
proposals.rationale: R30 names the specific assumption that item-space granularity should equal user-interest granularity and argues why that is wrong, and R59 names the exact failure mode of 'compounding errors in skill chaining' -- both dense_high_card_low. Contrast with generic underperformance claims typical in dense_low_card_high items like R27.

proposals.name: Fundamental vs. incremental significance of the question
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on how foundational or long-standing the stated research question is, independent of how complex the proposed solution is. A 10: the abstract frames itself as addressing a fundamental, long-open, or widely-applicable question (e.g., a basic quantity in a field, a core theoretical puzzle). A 0: the abstract addresses a narrow, specific engineering sub-problem confined to one existing pipeline.
proposals.rationale: R09 tackles the long-elusive functional form of generalization error 'across scales', and R37 addresses the rate-distortion function, called 'a key quantity in information theory' -- both dense_high_card_low. R10's three specific DNC bug-fixes and R17's three-stage colorization pipeline are narrow, pipeline-local engineering problems -- both dense_low_card_high.

proposals.name: Reframes the problem in more general/principled terms
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the abstract explicitly reformulates the target problem into a more general or more principled mathematical framing (e.g., casting a task as an optimization problem or a distributional-transport problem) rather than accepting the field's existing ad hoc problem statement. A 10: explicit reframing that generalizes the problem. A 0: the problem is taken as originally posed with no reframing.
proposals.rationale: R07 reframes molecular docking as 'a transport between distributions' and R29 reframes learned-Bloom-filter design as 'an optimization problem' -- both dense_high_card_low. R12 (SimulPL) and R03 keep the field's existing ad hoc problem framings and add engineering machinery on top -- both dense_low_card_high.

proposals.name: Information density relative to abstract length
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on the ratio of substantive, specific scientific content to total abstract length. A 10: every sentence adds a distinct, concrete claim or fact; no filler, throat-clearing, or repeated restatement of motivation. A 0: the abstract is long relative to its actual content, with generic filler sentences, repeated motivational framing, or padding that adds no new information.
proposals.rationale: R55 (five terse sentences stating a bold architectural claim) and R34 and R05 are short and conceptually dense with no wasted sentences -- all dense_high_card_low. R12 (SimulPL) and R51 (ProactiveBench) are long, enumerate many sub-parts, and repeat motivational framing across several sentences -- both dense_low_card_high.

proposals.name: Density of distinctly-named artifacts introduced
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on how many separately-named systems, datasets, benchmarks, or methods are introduced and described within the single abstract (count distinct proper-noun/acronym artifacts). A 10: three or more separately named artifacts (e.g., a dataset name, a method name, and a benchmark name) are each introduced and described. A 0: zero or one named artifact; the contribution is described in plain descriptive language rather than branded names.
proposals.rationale: R11 introduces PERSONALITYBENCH, a neuron-identification method, and an induction method as three named artifacts, and R51 introduces ProactiveBench plus a reward model plus a fine-tuned model -- both dense_low_card_high. R55 and R34 introduce zero or one named artifact -- both dense_high_card_low.

proposals.name: Breadth-of-evaluation-settings emphasized as evidence
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on how much the abstract leans on the SHEER NUMBER of models, datasets, tasks, or settings tested as its primary evidence of quality, rather than depth of analysis on one setting. A 10: the abstract enumerates many models/datasets/settings and cites counts (e.g., '22 open-source and 6 closed-source models', 'three language pairs at all latency levels'). A 0: the abstract discusses one setting, model, or theoretical construction in depth with no breadth-counting language.
proposals.rationale: R19 (LOKI) foregrounds '22 open-source LMMs and 6 closed-source models' across '26 subcategories' and R46 explicitly enumerates generalization to 'higher AT budgets, partial poisoning, unseen model architectures, and stronger... defenses' -- both dense_low_card_high. R55 and R45 instead go deep on one architecture or one theoretical framework -- both dense_high_card_low.

proposals.name: Bare quantified wins without a stated mechanism
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the abstract's main evidence is a numeric performance gain (percentage, AP, error-rate reduction, etc.) presented with little or no accompanying explanation of the underlying reason the gain occurs. A 10: the abstract's payload is essentially 'we changed X and get +N% on benchmark Y' with no deeper why. A 0: the abstract offers a claim/insight with no reliance on a headline percentage number, or uses numbers only to illustrate a stated mechanism rather than stand alone as the evidence.
proposals.rationale: R10 leads with a bare '43%' error-rate improvement from three patches and R33 leads with '+4.1 AP' from two named distillation tricks with only shallow diagnosis -- both dense_low_card_high. R29 and R34 (dense_high_card_low) make their case with almost no headline percentages at all.

proposals.name: Precise scholarly positioning against a specific named prior claim
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the abstract cites and engages a SPECIFIC prior published result, taxonomy, or hypothesis by name/citation and explains exactly how the new work refines, tests, or extends that specific claim, rather than referencing 'prior work' generically. A 10: names a specific prior paper/finding/taxonomy and states precisely how the new result relates to it. A 0: references 'existing methods' or 'prior work' only generically with no specific named claim being engaged.
proposals.rationale: R05 explicitly refines the 'benign, tempered and catastrophic overfitting (cf. Mallinar et al. 2022)' taxonomy, and R20 explicitly tests and extends specific findings from Frankle et al. 2019, Gur-Ari et al. 2018, and Achille et al. 2019 -- both dense_high_card_low. R27 and R46 reference prior approaches only in generic categorical terms -- both dense_low_card_high.

proposals.name: Branding-first vs. question-first opening
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the abstract's opening sentences pose a research question, tension, or observed gap before naming any proposed system (10 = question/gap established first, method name introduced only afterward), versus opening by naming and describing a branded system/method as the organizing device before establishing why it is needed (0 = method-name-first).
proposals.rationale: R48 opens with 'A fundamental question in adversarial machine learning is whether...' before naming any method, and R59 opens by describing the mobile-manipulation problem before naming M3 -- both dense_high_card_low. R03 opens by naming 'UV-Attack' as its organizing device and R40 opens by naming 'SELF-PARAM' -- both dense_low_card_high.

proposals.name: Mechanism-explanation co-occurring with low artifact-branding
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on the JOINT presence of (a) an explicit causal/mechanistic explanation for the result AND (b) minimal branding of new named sub-artifacts (0-1 named systems/datasets in the abstract). A 10: the abstract explains a clear mechanism AND introduces no more than one named artifact. A 0: the abstract either gives no mechanistic explanation, or introduces three or more named sub-artifacts (or both) -- the 'engineering-checklist' signature rather than the 'single-insight' signature.
proposals.rationale: R34 gives a single mechanistic insight ('classifier can be fixed... with little or no loss') while introducing no named sub-artifacts, and R48 explains the label-uncertainty mechanism while introducing no separately branded pipeline components -- both dense_high_card_low. R11 and R51 pair engineering breadth with multiple named sub-artifacts rather than a single mechanism -- both dense_low_card_high.

proposals.name: Abstract length / verbosity
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate ONLY how long and verbose the abstract is (approximate word count / number of sentences relative to a typical abstract in this pool), where 0 = extremely terse (a few short sentences) and 10 = extremely long and elaborated (many sentences, multiple paragraphs). Do not judge whether the length is appropriate or whether the paper is good; score length alone.
proposals.rationale: Row R52 (dense_pct=0.999, card_pct=0.006) is a 3-sentence, ~55-word abstract, while R38 (card_pct=0.972) and R08 (card_pct=0.960) run to elaborated multi-clause paragraphs enumerating several contributions; raw length/verbosity plausibly drives scorecard totals up (more text for each criterion to hook onto) independent of quality.

proposals.name: Quantitative superiority-claim density
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate ONLY how many explicit numeric comparison claims the abstract states (percentages, 'Nx faster/better', point-improvements over a named baseline), where 0 = no numbers/comparisons stated and 10 = many such numeric claims packed in. Do not judge whether the numbers are impressive, correct, or meaningful -- count/density only.
proposals.rationale: R33 ('92.7% attack success rate... significantly outperforming... 28.5% ASR', '49.5% ASR') and R46 ('43.9 AP... which is 4.1 higher than the baseline') both pack in explicit numeric wins and both sit at high card_pct (.809, .913), while R52 (card_pct=.006) states no such numbers at all.

proposals.name: Hype / superlative adjective density
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate ONLY how much the abstract uses superlative or hype adjectives/adverbs ('novel', 'significantly', 'remarkably', 'state-of-the-art', 'surprisingly', 'notably'), where 0 = plain, unembellished description and 10 = heavy use of such intensifiers. Do not judge whether the intensifiers are warranted -- count usage only.
proposals.rationale: R14 ('Remarkably, in more than 60% of cases human evaluators prefer...') and R49 ('Notably, our approach achieves...') both lean on intensifier words and both sit at very high card_pct (.869 and .995), while several lower-card rows in the slice state findings more flatly with no comparable intensifiers.

proposals.name: Raw math/LaTeX markup leakage
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate ONLY how much unrendered LaTeX/math markup or dense inline-citation apparatus appears in the visible text (literal backslash commands, '$...$' expressions, strings of parenthetical citations like '(Author, Year; Author2, Year2)'), where 0 = clean prose with no such markup and 10 = heavily interspersed with raw markup/citation strings. Do not judge the underlying math or the citations' relevance -- score visible markup density only.
proposals.rationale: R28 ('$\tilde O(\epsilon^{-2})$', '$O(\epsilon^{-3})$') and R43 ('(Gibson, 2017)', '(Blahut, 1972; Arimoto, 1972)', '(Balle et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2022)') both show heavy raw markup/citation-string leakage into the abstract text; this is a text-capture/typesetting-habit artifact rather than a direct quality signal.

proposals.name: Persistent project-page fingerprint
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate ONLY how much the abstract's link(s) look like a maintained, custom-domain project page (e.g., a lab or author subdomain hosting a dedicated results page) as opposed to a bare code-repository link, a generic shortener, or no link at all, where 0 = no link or only a shortener/bare-repo link and 10 = a clearly dedicated, custom-branded project page. Do not judge how good the linked content is -- score only how 'dedicated-project-page-like' the URL/mention looks.
proposals.rationale: R01 links to 'ali-design.github.io/gan_steerability' and R34 links to 'tau-vailab.github.io/ProtoSnap', both dedicated lab-branded project pages, versus R60 which links only via a generic 'bit.ly/marl-lipo' shortener; a dedicated page fingerprints an author/lab's established practice and resourcing in this format, not the research content itself.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practice in the format (lab/author web-presence and resourcing)

proposals.name: Ordinal contribution scaffold
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate ONLY how much the abstract uses an explicit ordinal/enumerative scaffold to walk through its content ('First, ... Second, ... Third, ...', 'Firstly, ... Finally, ...', or an equivalent numbered sequence of steps/contributions), where 0 = no such scaffold, free-flowing prose and 10 = a fully enumerated, ordinal structure. Do not judge whether the enumerated content itself is good -- score only the presence/strength of the ordinal scaffold.
proposals.rationale: R42 ('First, we study the role of normalization... Second, we study the role of network capacity...') and R58 ('First, we use synthetic language modeling tasks... Next, to improve the efficiency...') both impose an explicit ordinal walk-through; this scaffold fingerprints a particular drafting/editing template rather than the underlying work's merit.

proposals.name: Bolded key-term enumeration
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate ONLY how much the abstract uses bolded/emphasized inline terms to name and enumerate distinct aspects, categories, or contributions (e.g., '**Efficacy**', '**latency preference**'), where 0 = no such emphasis markup and 10 = multiple bolded terms used to structure the abstract's content. Do not judge whether the named categories are well-chosen -- score only the presence/density of this emphasis-enumeration device.
proposals.rationale: R27 bolds '**Efficacy**' and '**Retention**' as named factors and R39 bolds five separate categories ('**translation quality preference**', '**monotonicity preference**', '**key point preference**', '**simplicity preference**', '**latency preference**'); this markdown-emphasis convention fingerprints a drafting tool or editing-assistance practice, not research substance.

proposals.name: Hedged vs. assertive epistemic stance
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate ONLY how assertive/confirmed (vs. hedged/speculative) the abstract's stated findings sound, where 0 = heavily hedged language ('we hypothesize', 'may', 'suggests', 'remains an open question') and 10 = fully assertive, confirmed-result language ('achieves state-of-the-art', 'demonstrates', 'outperforms'). Do not judge whether the hedging or assertiveness is epistemically justified -- score only the surface stance.
proposals.rationale: R01 ('We hypothesize that the degree of distributional shift is related to...') and R37 ('it remains an open question whether...', 'We test the hypothesis that...') both lean heavily hedged, while many other rows in the slice state results in fully assertive terms; stance/confidence language can reflect where in the write-up or submission process a paper sits rather than the work's actual merit.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practice / stage of process (draft vs. confirmed-result framing)

proposals.name: Benchmark/dataset name-dropping density
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate ONLY how many named, widely-recognized standard benchmarks or datasets are mentioned by name in the abstract (e.g., ImageNet, CIFAR, COCO, SuperGLUE, D4RL, MuJoCo), where 0 = no named standard benchmarks/datasets and 10 = many named standard benchmarks/datasets referenced. Do not judge whether the benchmarks were used well -- count named mentions only.
proposals.rationale: R25 names 'miniImageNet, CUB-200, and CIFAR-100' and R51 names 'D4RL' alongside baselines 'MOPO', 'MOReL' and 'COMBO'; reciting the standard benchmark roster of a subfield fingerprints an author's familiarity with and practiced adherence to that community's format conventions, not the work's own quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practice in the format (subfield community convention / benchmark-suite familiarity)

proposals.name: Field-opening vs. prior-work-differentiating framing
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate ONLY how much the abstract's OPENING reads as a sweeping, first-principles framing of an entire problem/field (as if staking out one of the first obvious takes) versus how much it reads as explicitly cataloguing and differentiating itself from a list of specific prior methods (as if written after the obvious takes were already on the table), where 0 = pure sweeping field-level framing with no named prior-method contrast and 10 = opens by listing/contrasting specific prior approaches before introducing its own. Do not judge which framing is more rigorous -- score only which style the opening uses.
proposals.rationale: R01 opens with a sweeping field-level claim ('An open secret in contemporary machine learning is that many models work beautifully on standard benchmarks but fail to generalize...') with no prior-method catalogue, while R55 opens by contrasting itself against 'current factuality enhancement methods' and R39 opens by cataloguing what 'existing methods focus solely on... ignoring...'; this opening style plausibly fingerprints where an entry falls in the stream of takes on a topic.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream (order of this take relative to already-articulated prior takes)

proposals.name: Mechanistic Fit to the Bottleneck
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract identifies a specific failure and introduces a mechanism directly matched to it; score 0 when the method is generic or its connection to the stated problem is unclear.
proposals.rationale: R09 links specific SSM failures to H3 and FlashConv, while R21 links normalization changes to the clean/adversarial domain mismatch. These dense-high items make the problem-to-mechanism connection unusually explicit.

proposals.name: Explanatory Diagnostic Depth
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the work explains why a phenomenon occurs and tests predictions that distinguish the explanation; score 0 when it only reports aggregate performance improvements.
proposals.rationale: R14 constructs and analyzes a minimal example of edge-of-stability, and R25 decomposes weight balancing into identifiable effects. By contrast, R05 mainly reports AP gains after adding components.

proposals.name: Theory–Algorithm Closure
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when formal assumptions, guarantees or complexity bounds directly characterize the proposed algorithm and its use; score 0 when theory is absent or disconnected from the practical method.
proposals.rationale: R07 connects misaligned-gradient assumptions to explicit iteration complexities, while R46 turns an information-theoretic limit into an executable estimator. This tight closure is underrepresented in more benchmark-oriented abstracts such as R04.

proposals.name: Stress-Tested Transfer
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the claim is tested across genuinely unseen tasks, distributions, architectures, poses or operating conditions; score 0 when evaluation remains confined to one familiar in-domain setting.
proposals.rationale: R15 tests held-out agent environments, R47 tests unseen human poses and black-box detectors, and R19 evaluates structured exploration across task families. These abstracts foreground transfer conditions rather than only standard benchmarks.

proposals.name: Constraint-Aware Efficiency
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract identifies a concrete resource constraint and demonstrates reduced computation, memory, latency or data demands while retaining the intended capability; score 0 when resource costs are ignored.
proposals.rationale: R29 targets homomorphic-encryption cost, R39 removes a large classifier layer, and R43 reports substantially shorter training. Such explicit practical tradeoffs are less visible in broad performance claims such as R10.

proposals.name: Domain-Valid Inductive Bias
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the representation or architecture encodes a domain symmetry, geometry, interaction law or physical constraint and explains why that structure is appropriate; score 0 when the architecture is domain-agnostic without justification.
proposals.rationale: R27 builds exact symmetry into frame averaging, R52 represents directional long-range interactions, and R45 generates molecules from realistic structural motifs. These domain-aligned choices are strong quality signals beyond generic architectural novelty.

proposals.name: Semantically Controlled Intervention
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the method changes an interpretable internal factor and verifies a predictable, feasible behavioral change across intervention strengths or held-out conditions; score 0 when it merely correlates representations with labels.
proposals.rationale: R28 derives control vectors and checks feasibility and scaling behavior, while R56 identifies and manipulates personality-related neurons with trait-specific evaluation. This distinguishes actionable representation understanding from superficial probing.

proposals.name: Reusable Abstraction
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the proposed principle is stated at a reusable level and applies across architectures, tasks or symmetry types with clear conditions; score 0 when it is a bespoke solution for one narrowly defined setup.
proposals.rationale: R06 extends a 2D foundation-model idea to 3D point clouds, R27 adapts backbones to multiple symmetry types, and R52 integrates several interaction regimes. Their abstractions explain reuse rather than merely listing experiments.

proposals.name: Diagnostic Benchmark Design
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the evaluation varies modalities, difficulty, subskills or failure modes so that it diagnoses capability structure; score 0 when it uses one undifferentiated dataset and one headline metric.
proposals.rationale: R02 spans five modalities, difficulty levels and multiple question types, while R30 separates category levels and semantic relationships. These designs reveal what a system can and cannot do, unlike a single aggregate benchmark.

proposals.name: Supervision Provenance and Coverage
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract clearly explains how data, annotations or pseudo-labels are obtained and shows coverage of rare, unseen or practically important cases; score 0 when supervision is opaque, narrow or weakly connected to the claim.
proposals.rationale: R20 provides expert annotations and emphasizes rare signs, R02 describes curated multimodal questions with explicit subcategories, and R38 grounds proactive-agent data in real activities and human judgments. These details distinguish substantive data construction from dataset naming alone.

proposals.name: Boundary-Value Insight
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the work identifies an important failure, tradeoff or limitation and derives a useful implication from it; score 0 when it presents only uniformly positive claims without clarifying where the method or phenomenon breaks.
proposals.rationale: R35 shows that object tracking does not imply implicit logic, R44 maps the limits of GAN steerability, and R58 exposes a factuality/context-faithfulness tradeoff. Such negative or boundary findings are valuable evidence of research judgment.

proposals.name: Confound Isolation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when comparisons, controls or ablations separate competing explanations for the observed effect; score 0 when several factors change together and the claimed cause cannot be isolated from the abstract.
proposals.rationale: R21 separates clean and adversarial normalization statistics, R25 decomposes weight balancing into distinct mechanisms, and R30 tests whether interference depends on semantic relatedness. These controls support causal interpretation rather than association.

proposals.name: Compositional System Coherence
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when interacting components are designed to preserve global consistency or avoid compounding errors and are evaluated jointly on long-horizon or structured tasks; score 0 when modules are simply concatenated and assessed only locally.
proposals.rationale: R48 explicitly addresses skill-chaining errors through mobile skills and region goals, R22 balances global structure with local texture, and R59 models compositional interactions among user-interest facets. Their quality depends on interactions, not isolated components.

proposals.name: Validity-Aware Generation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when generation or control incorporates domain validity constraints during construction and checks them beyond a proxy task metric; score 0 when outputs are judged only by nominal accuracy or unconstrained scores.
proposals.rationale: R13 enforces energetically favorable molecular poses, R45 builds molecules from realistic motifs and valid geometry, and R50 evaluates learned control in real robotic manipulation. These works treat validity as part of the problem definition.

proposals.name: Evidence Triangulation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when complementary evidence types—such as theory, synthetic tests, scaling studies, real data and qualitative analysis—independently support the same claim; score 0 when evidence relies on one metric or one narrow benchmark.
proposals.rationale: R09 combines synthetic capability tests, language modeling, efficiency measurements and downstream tasks, while R50 combines theory, simulation, real-robot evaluation and ablations. R46 similarly joins artificial and real sources with rate-distortion analysis.

proposals.name: Promotional novelty rhetoric
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, judge how much the abstract uses superlatives, novelty claims, urgency, or emphatic success language; assess visible wording only, never whether the claims are deserved or indicate research quality.
proposals.rationale: Such rhetoric can attract attention or affect textual priors without measuring research quality. It is prominent in R03, R29, R30, and R41.

proposals.name: Acronym and branding load
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, judge how much the abstract uses coined method names, dense acronyms, unusual capitalization, or branded benchmarks; assess only their visible presence, never whether the naming is good or scientifically justified.
proposals.rationale: Memorable labels can improve recognition independently of substance. Examples include SELF-PARAM in R07, UV-Attack in R29, PERSONALITYBENCH in R46, and DirectCLR in R50.

proposals.name: Quantified result emphasis
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, judge how much the abstract foregrounds exact percentages, decimal measurements, benchmark deltas, or numerical comparisons; assess reporting density only, never whether the numbers are impressive or valid.
proposals.rationale: Some authors habitually foreground precise numerical evidence, which can affect reception while only imperfectly reflecting quality. This pattern appears in R29, R30, R43, and R48.

proposals.name: Artifact-release signaling
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, judge how much the abstract advertises code, data, models, checkpoints, or project pages; assess only the extent of release signaling, never whether the artifacts are useful or reproducible.
proposals.rationale: Artifact signaling can shape reader expectations independently of the underlying contribution, while the same practice may also accompany genuine engineering quality. It appears in R05, R15, R27, and R54.

proposals.name: Citation-format density
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, judge how much the abstract contains inline citations, author-year references, named prior methods, or reference-like parentheticals; assess formatting density only, never whether the literature positioning is appropriate.
proposals.rationale: Different communities use citation-heavy prose differently, creating stylistic priors unrelated to research quality. Dense examples include R05, R11, R39, and R56.

proposals.name: Problem-solution template cadence
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, judge how strongly the abstract follows a stock sequence of problem, limitations, proposed method, and experimental confirmation; assess rhetorical structure only, never whether the argument or method is good.
proposals.rationale: Template familiarity can make prose easier to parse without establishing scientific merit. The cadence is visible in R06, R24, R25, and R49.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practice in the abstract format

proposals.name: Extraction and formatting noise
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, judge how much the text contains broken words, odd whitespace, malformed links, duplicated fragments, raw markup, or layout artifacts; assess visible textual noise only, never whether the underlying work is good.
proposals.rationale: Parsing noise can alter how text is represented without belonging to the research itself. Examples include broken words in R07 and R55, duplicated text in R15 and R37, and layout artifacts in R39.

proposals.name: Recency and fashion markers
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, judge how much the abstract uses strongly time-coded topics, model names, benchmark versions, or currently fashionable application language; assess temporal salience only, never whether the topic is important or the work is high quality.
proposals.rationale: Production timing and fashionable terminology can influence textual priors, while access to newer tools or ideas may also affect genuine work quality. Clear markers occur in R07, R18, R22, R46, and R54.

proposals.name: Late-riff synthesis signature
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, judge how much the abstract reads as a layered recombination of several established paradigms, with multiple analogies, extensions, or hybrid components; assess only the textual synthesis pattern, never whether the synthesis is insightful or valuable.
proposals.rationale: A later entrant may have seen obvious framings and produce a more layered textual riff; that exposure can also affect genuine research development. This fingerprint appears in R09, R35, R54, and R59.

proposals.name: Formulaic polished fluency
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, judge how much the prose has highly regular sentence cadence, generic transitions, uniform polish, and low authorial idiosyncrasy; assess stylistic regularity only, never whether the writing or research is good.
proposals.rationale: Editing or assistance can make abstracts uniformly fluent without changing the research contribution, and stylistic smoothness can influence textual processing. The pattern is visible in R18, R24, R49, and R54.

proposals.name: Failure-Mechanism Fit
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract identifies a concrete failure mechanism and the proposed design directly addresses that mechanism; score 0 when it states a generic problem and adds an unmotivated technique.
proposals.rationale: R04 diagnoses noisy addressing, aliasing, and linkage degradation before matching each to a specific fix. R14 identifies recall and comparison deficits in SSMs and designs H3 around those capabilities.

proposals.name: Theory-to-Method Closure
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when formal analysis produces a concrete algorithm, design rule, or guarantee with clearly stated assumptions; score 0 when theory is decorative, disconnected from the method, or absent.
proposals.rationale: R12 constructs an analytically tractable example whose dynamics explain the observed phenomenon. R15 turns correlated-gradient analysis into algorithms with explicit complexity regimes.

proposals.name: Unifying Abstraction Across Regimes
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when one clearly defined principle explains or operates across genuinely different settings, with the mapping between settings made explicit; score 0 when multiple applications are merely listed without a shared abstraction.
proposals.rationale: R18 uses frame averaging for several symmetry families while preserving a common formal guarantee. R46 transfers neural rendering ideas from vision into wireless propagation through an explicit path-based analogy.

proposals.name: Interaction-Explicit Representation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the representation separately models multiple meaningful factors and their interactions, with an operational mechanism for composition; score 0 when all factors are collapsed into an undifferentiated representation.
proposals.rationale: R07 separates item facets from user-interest granularity and explicitly composes interests through binding. R53 represents directional, long-range, environmental, and graph interactions within an anisotropic state.

proposals.name: Exactness with Efficient Realization
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract establishes an exact structural property while replacing an otherwise impractical computation with a substantially simpler realization; score 0 when exactness is only asserted empirically or efficiency is unexamined.
proposals.rationale: R18 replaces intractable group averaging with frames while retaining exact invariance or equivariance. R49 formulates learned Bloom-filter utilization as an optimization problem yielding near-optimal procedures.

proposals.name: Surprising Finding, Mechanistic Explanation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract reports a counterintuitive phenomenon and then supplies a principled explanation or diagnostic model for it; score 0 when it reports an unexpected observation without explaining why it occurs.
proposals.rationale: R19 explains exponential learning-rate behavior through normalization and parameter equivalence. R51 connects unexpected adversarial-training behavior to mixed-domain normalization statistics and capacity.

proposals.name: Joint Constraint Awareness
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the method simultaneously incorporates several real constraints that interact in deployment, and the design explicitly manages their trade-offs; score 0 when practical constraints are mentioned only as background or measured one at a time.
proposals.rationale: R08 jointly addresses reachability, navigation endpoints, and long-horizon skill chaining. R43 combines model uncertainty, model-free estimates, and conservative policy evaluation in one offline-RL design.

proposals.name: Reusable Scientific Primitive
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the contribution is a clearly scoped primitive that can be reused across architectures, domains, or downstream tasks through the same mechanism; score 0 when it is a narrowly tailored pipeline with no evident reuse beyond its benchmark.
proposals.rationale: R25 develops a kernel family with theoretical links and applications across implicit surface reconstruction settings. R60 turns promptable segmentation and a data engine into a reusable 3D foundation-style capability across multiple scene types.

proposals.name: Construct Validity and Confound Separation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract defines the target construct and tests it against plausible alternative explanations or confounds; score 0 when the proposed metric or benchmark measures an ambiguous proxy without disambiguation.
proposals.rationale: R20 distinguishes object tracking from the separate logical generalization being tested. R24 explicitly tests whether language-image interference reflects shared semantics or mere dominance of the word representation.

proposals.name: Causal Attribution in Evaluation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when controlled comparisons, ablations, or intervention-based tests isolate which component causes each claimed effect; score 0 when the abstract offers only aggregate comparisons with no component-level attribution.
proposals.rationale: R02 includes asymptotic analysis, intervention-model variation, and ablations tied to its proposed explanation. R11 progressively removes diffusion components to identify which elements actually matter for representation learning.
