proposals.name: Targeted Distribution-Shift Testing
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when evaluation deliberately targets the stated failure mode using unseen environments, perturbations, poses, domains, or tasks; score 0 when evaluation remains confined to routine in-distribution benchmarks.
proposals.rationale: R17 evaluates held-out agent environments and perturbations tied to its generalization claim. R22 tests unseen actions, poses, views, and black-box detectors rather than only familiar attack conditions.

proposals.name: Data and Benchmark Stewardship
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract explains data provenance, annotation procedures, coverage, leakage controls, and important limitations; score 0 when it mainly gives dataset size or a repository link without describing data quality or validity.
proposals.rationale: R16 addresses human-annotated data, subjective evaluation, strategic manipulation, and contamination. R28 describes expert annotations, rare-sign coverage, structural priors, and released data for a specialized benchmark.

proposals.name: Claim Calibration and Limitations
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when claims are carefully scoped and the abstract states trade-offs, failure cases, or conditions under which the method may not work; score 0 when broad superiority or applicability is asserted without boundaries.
proposals.rationale: R20 explicitly reports that models acquire structural similarity yet fail the intended logic test. R54 presents a factuality/context-faithfulness trade-off and identifies conditions where enhancement methods deteriorate behavior.

proposals.name: Resource Accounting for Practicality
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when computational cost, memory, latency, data requirements, or deployment constraints are quantified alongside the claimed capability; score 0 when efficiency or practicality is asserted without resource accounting.
proposals.rationale: R29 makes encryption-related fine-tuning and inference costs central and quantifies both. R14 connects hardware utilization, sequence length, training speed, and generation speed to its architectural choices.

proposals.name: Reproducibility Protocol Completeness
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract provides artifacts plus enough methodological, data, and evaluation detail to make replication realistically actionable; score 0 when the method and evaluation protocol remain too vague even if a code link is mentioned.
proposals.rationale: R26 identifies architecture stages, evaluation modes, released code, and checkpoints. R50 specifies probe geometry, target structures, comparison space, evaluation focus, and a reproducible implementation.

proposals.name: Release-infrastructure cues
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how much the abstract advertises code, data, models, checkpoints, videos, or project pages; judge presence only, never whether release is good.
proposals.rationale: R03, R05, R11, R12, and R30 prominently advertise repositories, videos, data, models, or project pages. Such infrastructure reflects packaging and dissemination capacity, which can attract attention independently of underlying research quality; it may also support genuinely stronger work.

proposals.name: Acronym branding density
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how much the abstract uses invented method names, acronyms, branded datasets, or stylized model labels; judge only their presence, never whether the naming is good.
proposals.rationale: R07, R13, R18, and R39 contain multiple named components, benchmarks, or frameworks. Branding conventions can make an abstract more memorable without indicating research quality.

proposals.name: Numeric claim density
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how much the abstract foregrounds percentages, multipliers, timing figures, benchmark deltas, or explicit comparative claims; judge only textual density, never whether the claims are good.
proposals.rationale: R05, R08, R13, and R21 prominently use speedups, percentages, accuracy changes, and baseline comparisons. Numeric rhetoric is a presentation habit that can influence attention without itself establishing research quality.

proposals.name: Superlative novelty language
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how much the abstract uses words such as novel, first, universal, remarkable, superior, or state-of-the-art; judge only their extent, never whether the claims are justified.
proposals.rationale: R01, R07, R24, and R54 use expansive novelty, universality, superiority, or capability language. Such wording is persuasive framing rather than evidence of research quality.

proposals.name: Typesetting provenance artifacts
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how much the text contains broken hyphenation, malformed spacing, duplicated clauses or URLs, raw markup, or conversion artifacts; judge only visible irregularities, never their quality implications.
proposals.rationale: R03 and R29 show broken word wrapping, while R30, R33, and R51 contain duplicated material or unusual formatting. These artifacts can reflect submission processing or editing history and affect readability independently of research quality.

proposals.name: Formula-jargon compression
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how much the abstract relies on dense notation, nested technical terminology, acronyms, or compressed mathematical claims with little plain-language unpacking; judge extent only, never whether the exposition is good.
proposals.rationale: R20, R27, R47, and R57 compress substantial arguments into notation-heavy language. Disciplinary writing practice can influence reception independently of quality, while practiced technical authorship may also accompany genuinely stronger research.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practice in the abstract format

proposals.name: Trend-platform anchoring
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how much the abstract foregrounds fashionable platforms, model families, or topical labels such as LLMs, agents, CLIP, SAM, diffusion, or NeRF; judge only textual prominence, never whether the topic is good.
proposals.rationale: R05, R10, R18, R22, R39, and R44 prominently anchor their framing in currently salient model families or application trends. Audience targeting and field fashion can shape attention without determining quality, though access to active communities and feedback can also support better research.

proposals.name: Template-shaped exposition
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how much the abstract follows a stock problem-gap-method-experiments-conclusion scaffold with generic connective phrases; judge only structural regularity, never whether the writing or research is good.
proposals.rationale: R04, R10, R39, and R49 use highly recognizable contribution templates and stock transitions. Template fluency can reflect editorial assistance or community convention, making it predictive of presentation effects without being research quality itself.
proposals.upstream_parent: editing or assistance using field templates

proposals.name: Crowded-stream positioning
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how much the abstract reads as a response to an already crowded line of work, using framing such as recent, existing, consensus, revisit, gap, challenge, or first attempt; judge only the framing, never whether it is insightful.
proposals.rationale: R08, R17, R40, and R52 explicitly invoke consensus, recent developments, prior limitations, or an established problem context. Submission timing and container position can leave this textual fingerprint, affecting contextual salience independently of research quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream and submission timing

proposals.name: Benchmark-catalogue breadth
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how much the abstract lists datasets, environments, modalities, domains, baselines, or downstream applications; judge only the amount of enumeration, never whether breadth is valuable.
proposals.rationale: R07, R21, and R44 enumerate many tasks, datasets, modalities, or subcategories, while R54 lists numerous downstream uses. Benchmark culture can reward breadth as a stylistic signal independent of quality, although genuine breadth may also reflect substantive research strength.
proposals.upstream_parent: community or venue norms around breadth demonstrations

proposals.name: Conceptual over Empirical Framing
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract is dedicated to defining a novel conceptual framework or theoretical insight, with empirical work serving only as secondary validation. Score 0 if the abstract is driven entirely by empirical results, benchmark scores, and engineering improvements without proposing a new underlying concept.
proposals.rationale: Dense-favored abstracts like R10 and R21 introduce broad conceptual frameworks (e.g., 2-simplicial attention, Frame Averaging), while scorecard-favored abstracts like R16 and R23 focus heavily on empirical performance gains and task-specific tuning. The dense model seems to credit fundamental conceptual leaps over pure empirical benchmarking.

proposals.name: Explicit Mathematical Rigor
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract explicitly mentions formal theorems, rigorous proofs, convergence bounds, or complex mathematical derivations. Score 0 if the abstract contains absolutely no formal theoretical claims, bounds, or mathematical analysis.
proposals.rationale: The dense model highly favors rigorous theoretical formulations, as seen in the bounds on misaligned gradients in R22 and the eigenstructure analysis in R43. In contrast, scorecard-favored abstracts (R45, R30) generally omit formal mathematical guarantees, which the dense model likely perceives as a lack of depth.

proposals.name: Cross-Domain Generality of Core Insight
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the core contribution is a universal principle, mathematical operator, or framework applicable across many distinct domains and architectures. Score 0 if the contribution is an ad-hoc, narrow engineering tweak applicable only to a highly specific task or dataset.
proposals.rationale: Dense-favored abstracts propose highly general frameworks, such as exact invariance in R21 or analyzing the marginal value of the last layer in R48. Scorecard-favored abstracts target hyper-specific niches (e.g., cuneiform signs in R58, simultaneous MT in R35), which the dense model may penalize for lack of broad scientific impact.

proposals.name: Information Density and Conciseness
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract is highly concise, packing every sentence with novel technical constraints, formal definitions, or core algorithmic ideas without any filler. Score 0 if the abstract is verbose, padded with boilerplate text, exhaustive lists of datasets, or repetitive explanations.
proposals.rationale: Dense-favored abstracts like R02 and R10 are remarkably short and dense, delivering high information value per sentence. Conversely, scorecard-favored abstracts like R27 and R30 are verbose and padded with exhaustive lists of tasks and datasets, suggesting the dense model values a high signal-to-noise ratio.

proposals.name: Mechanistic Deconstruction over Black-Box Tuning
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract deconstructs an existing complex model or phenomenon to isolate and explain the exact causal factors of its behavior. Score 0 if the abstract treats the model as a black box, merely stacking new modules to improve output metrics.
proposals.rationale: The dense model highly credits works that reverse-engineer or explain underlying mechanics, such as deconstructing diffusion models to find they resemble classical autoencoders (R41) or analyzing early training dynamics (R34). Scorecard-favored abstracts (R19, R16) just add modules to black boxes, missing what the dense model perceives as true mechanistic understanding.

proposals.name: Counter-Intuitive or Paradigm-Challenging Insight
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the main finding explicitly challenges a standard assumption or overturns conventional wisdom (e.g., proving a widely used component is unnecessary). Score 0 if the work represents a predictable, incremental progression of existing methods.
proposals.rationale: Dense-favored abstracts (R48, R03) present surprising, counter-intuitive discoveries that challenge current practices. Scorecard-favored abstracts (R26, R45) follow predictable, safe trends. The dense model appears to value paradigm-challenging insights highly.

proposals.name: Absence of Hype and Marketing Language
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the tone is strictly objective, technical, and completely devoid of subjective superlatives. Score 0 if it is filled with marketing-style hype phrases like 'unprecedented scale,' 'paves the way,' or 'significantly outperforms.'
proposals.rationale: Dense-favored abstracts (R06, R22) maintain a dry, strictly technical tone. Scorecard-favored abstracts (R01, R04) frequently rely on promotional language ('paves the way,' 'significantly outperforms'). The dense model likely penalizes marketing fluff, whereas the scorecard might erroneously score it as confidence or impact.

proposals.name: First-Principles Problem Formulation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the problem is formulated from fundamental definitions, physical laws, or basic mathematical axioms rather than heuristic observations. Score 0 if the problem is formulated merely as an ad-hoc engineering pipeline bottleneck.
proposals.rationale: Dense-favored abstracts (R33, R40) formulate problems from first principles (e.g., rate-distortion limits, transport between distributions). Scorecard-favored ones (R37, R14) tackle ad-hoc engineering challenges. The dense model credits fundamental physical or mathematical formulations.

proposals.name: Exact Mathematical Guarantees over Heuristics
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the method explicitly provides mathematically exact properties (e.g., 'exact invariance,' 'provably optimal,' 'guaranteed bounds'). Score 0 if the method relies entirely on heuristic approximations, empirical validations, and probabilistic guesses.
proposals.rationale: Dense-favored abstracts (R02, R21) highlight exact guarantees (near-optimal performance, exact equivariance). Scorecard-favored ones (R51, R16) rely on heuristic adjustments. The dense model strongly prefers provable exactness over heuristic tuning.

proposals.name: Minimalist Solution and Occam's Razor
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract demonstrates that a drastically simpler, more elegant, or stripped-down approach is mathematically or empirically equivalent to complex state-of-the-art pipelines. Score 0 if the proposed solution involves stacking multiple complex modules, custom losses, or intricate training stages.
proposals.rationale: Dense-favored abstracts (R41, R48) emphasize simplicity, showing that complex modern components are nonessential. Scorecard-favored abstracts (R35, R46) add complex pipelines and combinations of techniques. The dense model seems to highly value the intellectual elegance of minimalism.

proposals.name: Unification of Disparate Concepts
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the core contribution unifies previously unconnected ideas, algorithms, or frameworks under a single coherent theoretical formulation. Score 0 if the work merely applies an existing isolated idea to a new dataset.
proposals.rationale: Dense-favored abstracts (R21, R33) unify distinct concepts (e.g., graph/point cloud symmetries via frame averaging, or molecular docking as a transport problem). Scorecard-favored abstracts (R26, R35) apply existing methods to new subfields. The dense model credits overarching unification.

proposals.name: Formal Trade-off Navigation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract formally defines and mathematically navigates a fundamental trade-off (e.g., bias vs. variance, exploration vs. exploitation, efficiency vs. accuracy). Score 0 if it ignores underlying trade-offs and simply claims absolute empirical improvement.
proposals.rationale: Dense-favored abstracts (R08, R22) explicitly navigate formal trade-offs (e.g., trading off model vs. model-free estimates based on uncertainty). Scorecard-favored abstracts (R56, R53) ignore formal trade-offs in favor of claiming absolute gains. The dense model recognizes the deep understanding required to formalize trade-offs.

proposals.name: Novel Inductive Bias over Pure Scaling
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the improvement is explicitly attributed to a novel structural prior, architectural inductive bias, or fundamental change in representation. Score 0 if the improvement relies entirely on more data, larger scale, or hyperparameter tuning.
proposals.rationale: Dense-favored abstracts (R10, R31) introduce fundamental changes to inductive biases (e.g., higher-dimensional attention, new sequence modeling layers). Scorecard-favored ones (R27, R45) focus on scaling and datasets. The dense model values structural innovation over brute-force scaling.

proposals.name: Identification of Hidden Flaws in Paradigms
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract explicitly diagnoses a subtle, previously unrecognized flaw, mathematical instability, or conceptual bottleneck in widely used standard methods. Score 0 if it simply builds on top of standard paradigms without questioning their foundations.
proposals.rationale: Dense-favored abstracts (R18, R34) identify hidden flaws in standard setups (e.g., standard concentration ignoring label uncertainty, edge-of-stability dynamics). Scorecard-favored ones (R07, R19) do not diagnose underlying flaws. The dense model rewards foundational critique.

proposals.name: Geometric or Information-Theoretic Grounding
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the core method is deeply grounded in information theory, Riemannian geometry, spatial topology, or physical constraints. Score 0 if the method lacks any grounding in advanced mathematical physics, geometry, or information theory.
proposals.rationale: Dense-favored abstracts (R06, R40) are deeply rooted in geometry and information theory. Scorecard-favored ones (R04, R30) lack this mathematical grounding. The dense model seems to explicitly favor methods grounded in fundamental theories of information and space.

proposals.name: Abstract Length Brevity
proposals.instruction: Score from 0 (very long) to 10 (very short) based strictly on the word count of the abstract text. Do not judge the quality of the length, only measure how brief it is.
proposals.rationale: Length can arbitrarily bias a scorecard model that rewards completeness, while a dense model might penalize excessively short abstracts that fail to fully explain the methodology (e.g., the very brief R15 versus the more standard length of R02).

proposals.name: Trendy Buzzword Density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on the extent to which the abstract features current highly-saturated machine learning buzzwords (e.g., 'LLM', 'agents', 'GPT'). Do not judge the validity of the research, only the presence of the terms.
proposals.rationale: Bandwagoning on trendy terms is an upstream community effect that might inflate a scorecard's perception of relevance, while the dense model implicitly discounts the hype (e.g., R03, R46).

proposals.name: Raw LaTeX Artifacts
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on the presence of un-compiled LaTeX formatting symbols (e.g., \texttt, $\times$, \cite) in the abstract text. Do not judge the quality of the work based on these artifacts.
proposals.rationale: Poorly compiled text reflects upstream editing or formatting failures that might not affect a scorecard model's criteria checkboxes, but could degrade a dense model's text processing (e.g., R41, R43).

proposals.name: Explicit URL Inclusion
proposals.instruction: Score 0 to 10 on how prominently raw URLs or web links are pasted into the abstract. Do not judge the usefulness of the code or link, only its textual presence.
proposals.rationale: Including links is a habit of certain subfields or labs. A dense model might read raw URLs as noise, whereas the card model might score it favorably under a heuristic for 'reproducibility' (e.g., R02, R37).

proposals.name: Obvious Concept Combination
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on the extent to which the paper reads as an obvious, formulaic combination of existing trendy concepts (e.g., 'Doing X for Y'). Do not assess the actual novelty or value of the idea.
proposals.rationale: Late-arriving entries in a research trend often adopt a highly predictable 'X applied to Y' template that reads perfectly to a scorecard but lacks the deep insight a dense model might look for (e.g., R17, R40).

proposals.name: Markdown Syntax Presence
proposals.instruction: Score 0 to 10 on the presence of Markdown formatting (like **bold** or *italics*) in the abstract text. Do not judge if the formatting is good or bad.
proposals.rationale: Non-standard Markdown formatting reveals an author's habit of copying from web pages or README files rather than using academic prose tools, which could bias a dense text model while being ignored by a scorecard (e.g., R17, R49).

proposals.name: Playful Title Extent
proposals.instruction: Score 0 to 10 on how playful, informal, or pun-based the title is (e.g., alliterations, pop-culture references). Do not judge the appropriateness of the title.
proposals.rationale: Catchy titles are an upstream social strategy to grab attention at conferences that the card model ignores, but the dense model might correlate such stylized choices with specific quality profiles (e.g., R16, R32).

proposals.name: Grandiosity of Claims
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on the extent of hyperbolic or grandiose language used to frame the problem or solution (e.g., 'paving the way', 'remarkable', 'open secret'). Do not judge the actual impact of the research.
proposals.rationale: Over-inflated claims are an upstream response to a crowded submission pool, potentially tricking a scorecard model into weighting the contribution heavily while being discounted by a dense model reading the actual semantics (e.g., R03, R05).

proposals.name: Decimal Benchmark Citing
proposals.instruction: Score 0 to 10 on the density of highly specific decimal-point metric improvements cited in the abstract (e.g., 66.47%, 116.4%). Do not judge if the improvements are actually significant.
proposals.rationale: Listing exact decimal points is a community style marker meant to satisfy reviewer process dynamics, which scorecards might reward as 'strong empirical results' but dense models might view as overfitting or marketing noise (e.g., R03, R38).
proposals.upstream_parent: process dynamics on the receiving side

proposals.name: Theory Jargon Density
proposals.instruction: Score 0 to 10 on the presence of dense, formal mathematical or theoretical terminology (e.g., 'Riemannian metric', 'Hadamard matrix'). Do not judge the correctness or difficulty of the theory.
proposals.rationale: Pure theory papers use dense jargon that dense models might implicitly associate with high-prestige venues, while scorecard models looking for standard empirical structures might score them lower (e.g., R07, R39).

proposals.name: Mechanistic Clarity of Proposed Solution
proposals.instruction: 10 = Abstract clearly identifies the precise mathematical, physical, or structural root cause of a problem and proposes a solution that explicitly targets it (e.g., R02, R30, R56); 0 = Abstract claims improvements through generic engineering or scaling without isolating a specific underlying mechanism (e.g., R01, R46).
proposals.rationale: The dense model strongly rewards papers that explain exactly *why* a method works, whereas the scorecard is easily impressed by black-box tuning and generic claims of superiority.

proposals.name: Parsimony and System Simplification
proposals.instruction: 10 = Abstract demonstrates that a complex method can be replaced by a significantly simpler, more elegant, or unified formulation without loss of power (e.g., R03, R14, R17); 0 = Abstract proposes a highly complex pipeline that merely stacks multiple techniques to achieve incremental gains (e.g., R20, R46).
proposals.rationale: The dense model values intellectual elegance and minimalism, while the scorecard over-credits engineering complexity and module stacking.

proposals.name: Fundamental Theoretical Contribution
proposals.instruction: 10 = Abstract centers on advancing core theoretical understanding via rigorous proofs, bounds, or characterizations of limits (e.g., R33, R35, R52, R58); 0 = Abstract is entirely empirical, with vague claims of 'theoretical analysis' but no specific fundamental contribution (e.g., R05, R49).
proposals.rationale: Pure theory papers with deep conceptual implications receive high scores from the dense model but may lack the standard empirical cues (like benchmark wins) that the scorecard looks for.

proposals.name: Problem Formulation Abstraction
proposals.instruction: 10 = Abstract reframes a narrow applied problem into a broader, solvable mathematical or conceptual abstraction (e.g., R27, R48); 0 = Abstract treats an applied problem purely as an ad-hoc sequence of domain-specific engineering steps (e.g., R25, R49).
proposals.rationale: The dense model highly values the intellectual leap of abstracting a specific problem into a general formalism, whereas the scorecard misses this conceptual depth.

proposals.name: Novel Mathematical Inductive Bias
proposals.instruction: 10 = Abstract introduces a novel, mathematically grounded inductive bias (e.g., symmetries, manifolds, tensor products) directly into the model architecture (e.g., R17, R19, R50); 0 = Abstract relies on standard, generic architectures with no explicit structural biases (e.g., R15, R53).
proposals.rationale: Integrating advanced mathematical structures into models is a strong signal of deep ML research quality that the scorecard misses in favor of standard benchmarking.

proposals.name: Methodological Depth Over Benchmark Proliferation
proposals.instruction: 10 = Primary contribution is a novel algorithm, architecture, or theory, with any datasets created purely as evaluation vehicles (e.g., R02, R17); 0 = Contribution revolves entirely around curating a new dataset, benchmark, or evaluation suite using standard methods (e.g., R08, R44, R54).
proposals.rationale: The scorecard seems to systematically over-credit benchmark/dataset papers, while the dense model prioritizes fundamental methodological and algorithmic innovations.

proposals.name: Diagnostic Precision of Failure Modes
proposals.instruction: 10 = Abstract pinpoints a highly specific, previously unrecognized mathematical or architectural flaw in existing methods (e.g., R02, R30); 0 = Abstract relies on vague critiques like 'poor generalization' or 'lack of understanding' without isolating the exact failure point (e.g., R01, R43).
proposals.rationale: Identifying the exact root cause of a failure is crucial; the dense model rewards this diagnostic precision while the scorecard may be swayed by broad problem statements.

proposals.name: Rigorous Algorithmic Formulation vs Anthropomorphism
proposals.instruction: 10 = Abstract formalizes its contribution using strict computational, statistical, or mathematical principles (e.g., R07, R27); 0 = Abstract relies on anthropomorphic, cognitive, or psychological terminology as the core conceptual contribution without rigorous formalization (e.g., R23, R39, R44).
proposals.rationale: The scorecard over-credits papers using trendy cognitive or behavioral buzzwords, whereas the dense model discounts them in favor of mathematical rigor.

proposals.name: Demystification and Deconstructive Analysis
proposals.instruction: 10 = Abstract systematically deconstructs a complex system to isolate the minimal necessary components, or reveals simple underlying dynamics (e.g., R14, R18); 0 = Abstract blindly builds upon complex, popular paradigms without questioning their foundational assumptions (e.g., R47).
proposals.rationale: The dense model highly rewards 'deconstructive' science that simplifies our understanding of ML, a subtle academic property missed by the scorecard.

proposals.name: Resolution of Fundamental Trade-offs
proposals.instruction: 10 = Abstract demonstrates a method that breaks a well-known trade-off (e.g., efficiency vs. accuracy) through a novel insight (e.g., R03, R27); 0 = Abstract merely shifts a trade-off slightly along the Pareto frontier using more data or compute (e.g., R13, R34).
proposals.rationale: Overcoming classical limits is a hallmark of exceptional research that the scorecard fails to recognize if standard metrics aren't heavily featured.

proposals.name: Cross-Domain Mathematical Concept Transfer
proposals.instruction: 10 = Abstract successfully maps a deep mathematical concept or physical law from another domain to solve an ML problem (e.g., R04, R19); 0 = Abstract merely applies a standard ML architecture to a new dataset or modality without fundamental adaptation (e.g., R16, R38).
proposals.rationale: The dense model captures the high intellectual value of transferring rigorous mathematical tools across domains, while the scorecard misses this in favor of surface-level application.

proposals.name: Quantification of Fundamental Limits
proposals.instruction: 10 = Abstract explicitly measures, bounds, or derives the fundamental theoretical limits of a model, data source, or algorithm (e.g., R31, R52, R58); 0 = Abstract focuses entirely on empirical SOTA-beating without considering fundamental theoretical bounds (e.g., R05, R49).
proposals.rationale: Establishing what is theoretically possible is a distinct quality marker that the dense model perceives but the scorecard overlooks.

proposals.name: Explicit Predictive Scaling Laws
proposals.instruction: 10 = Abstract provides a functional form or scaling law that allows reliable extrapolation of model behavior to unseen scales (e.g., R02, R30, R52); 0 = Abstract uses weak, qualitative claims of 'scalability' without explicit mathematical prediction (e.g., R60).
proposals.rationale: Dense models value theoretical predictions across scales, whereas scorecards might just check for the presence of large-scale experiments without verifying their predictive structure.

proposals.name: Utility of Geometric and Topological Insights
proposals.instruction: 10 = Abstract explicitly leverages geometric or topological properties (e.g., curvature, symmetries) to improve representations or training (e.g., R04, R17); 0 = Abstract treats data purely as flat, unstructured vectors, ignoring the geometry of the problem (e.g., R53).
proposals.rationale: The dense model identifies that utilizing geometric properties often yields fundamental improvements missed by standard algorithmic approaches.

proposals.name: Precision in Theoretical Claims
proposals.instruction: 10 = Abstract makes highly specific theoretical claims, citing exact iteration complexities, bounds, or equivalent formulations (e.g., R33, R35, R55); 0 = Abstract makes generic claims of 'theoretical guarantees' without specifying the nature, assumptions, or bounds of the result (e.g., R10).
proposals.rationale: The dense model distinguishes between rigorous, quantifiable theory and vague, hand-wavy theoretical posturing that the scorecard might equally credit.

proposals.name: Raw Markup Syntax Visibility
proposals.instruction: 0-10, how much raw markdown (e.g., **, ##) or LaTeX formatting syntax (e.g., \textbf{}, \url{}, \%) is visible in the abstract text? 0 means no raw syntax, 10 means heavily cluttered with it. Do not judge whether this formatting makes the text better or worse.
proposals.rationale: The presence of uncompiled LaTeX or raw markdown indicates copy-pasting from different source editors or web builders without cleaning the text. R35 and R52 feature heavy raw markdown bolding (e.g., **translation quality preference**), while R11 contains unformatted LaTeX percent signs (\%). This is a purely stylistic artifact of the drafting pipeline and not a measure of research quality.

proposals.name: Code Availability Link Verbosity
proposals.instruction: 0-10, to what extent does the abstract explicitly feature a URL or mention open-source code availability? 0 means no mention; 10 means prominent, repeated mentions of links and open-source availability. Do not judge if providing code is a good practice.
proposals.rationale: Including GitHub links or project pages is a sub-field norm or institutional template habit that leaves a strong textual fingerprint. R03 and R26 explicitly direct the reader to GitHub or project URLs at the very end. Models may mistake this standard boilerplate for a sign of a complete, high-quality empirical submission.

proposals.name: Trendy Topic Jargon Density
proposals.instruction: 0-10, to what extent does the abstract feature a high density of highly popular, trendy terms (e.g., 'LLMs', 'GPT-4', 'NeRF', 'CLIP')? 0 means none; 10 means the abstract is overwhelmingly packed with trendy jargon. Do not judge the actual quality of the research.
proposals.rationale: Authors often explicitly anchor their work to highly popular, trendy models or concepts to ride the wave of current research attention. R04 repeatedly mentions models like Llama-2 and OpenLLaMA, while R45 leans heavily on 'LLM Agents'. This acts as a temporal tell and audience hook that is predictive of visibility but not inherently tied to the underlying research quality.

proposals.name: Explicit Section Headers or Bullets
proposals.instruction: 0-10, how much does the abstract use explicit inline structural markers like bullet points, numbered lists, or bold inline headers? 0 means prose only; 10 means extensively segmented into bulleted or explicitly headed chunks. Do not judge if this structure improves readability.
proposals.rationale: Some authors apply a corporate or highly structured template to their abstracts, breaking standard academic prose into explicit lists. R03 uses '(1)... (2)' numbering to list reasons, and R38 uses bullet points ('• Training can be done...') to outline results. Models may favor this structured formatting without recognizing it as a mere stylistic choice.

proposals.name: Abstract Length and Verbosity
proposals.instruction: 0-10, how long and verbose is the abstract text? 0 is extremely short (e.g., a single brief paragraph) and 10 is exceptionally long and wordy. Do not judge if the length is appropriate.
proposals.rationale: Abstract length varies drastically independent of the core scientific contribution. R14 is exceptionally long and verbose, detailing multiple intricate experimental setups, whereas R58 is remarkably short and concise. Models often equate verbosity with thoroughness, making length a spurious predictive surface feature.

proposals.name: AI-Generation Stylistic Tics
proposals.instruction: 0-10, how heavily does the text contain stylistic tics typical of AI assistants (e.g., 'delve into', 'paves the way', 'garners attention', 'remarkable abilities')? 0 means none; 10 means pervasive AI-assistant phrasing. Do not judge if this writing style is good or bad.
proposals.rationale: The use of LLMs for editing or drafting abstracts leaves recognizable stylistic tics that can unconsciously bias a reader or model into perceiving the text as 'well-polished.' R35 and R45 both rely heavily on cliché AI phrasing like 'paving/paves the way for future advancements.' This is a fingerprint of the editing process, not the research itself.

proposals.name: Custom Project Acronym Density
proposals.instruction: 0-10, how many custom, project-specific acronyms (e.g., FLAG, NeRN, ImpScore) are introduced and repeated in the abstract? 0 means none; 10 means an overwhelming number of custom acronyms. Do not judge if the acronyms are clever.
proposals.rationale: Branding a method with a catchy, forced acronym is an upstream marketing habit meant to increase memorability. R28 introduces 'FLAG', and R50 introduces 'ImpScore', emphasizing the brand name over the method description. Models might score these highly due to memorability rather than scientific merit.

proposals.name: Exact Numeric Metric Reporting
proposals.instruction: 0-10, to what extent does the abstract cite specific, exact numeric performance improvements (e.g., 'by 43%', 'F1-Score of 66.47%')? 0 means no exact numbers; 10 means heavily populated with specific metrics. Do not judge whether the metrics are impressive.
proposals.rationale: Certain sub-fields norm on packing the abstract with exact quantitative gains, while others (like pure theory) use none. R03 cites exact numbers like '43.9 AP' and R05 reports '116.4%'. This acts as a sub-field marker that a model might misinterpret as a proxy for rigorous empirical validation, rather than just a reporting style.

proposals.name: Late-Arriving Contrarian Framing
proposals.instruction: 0-10, to what extent does the abstract read like a late-arriving reaction or explicit rebuttal to an already highly-publicized consensus or well-known model? 0 means a completely original framing; 10 means the entire premise is reacting to an established 'obvious take'. Do not judge if the contrarian stance is correct.
proposals.rationale: Abstracts often position themselves as late-arriving riffs that explicitly challenge a prevailing trend, leaving a fingerprint of contrarianism in the title and opening sentences. R11 ('Is Factuality Enhancement a Free Lunch?') and R55 ('Is Adversarial Training Really a Silver Bullet?') both frame their research as direct reactions to established consensus. This is a structural response to the existing literature stream rather than a measure of the paper's actual contribution.

proposals.name: Boilerplate Problem-Statement Phrasing
proposals.instruction: 0-10, to what extent does the text rely on standard boilerplate problem-statement phrasing (e.g., 'has gained importance because', 'has been proved as an effective technique')? 0 means completely original phrasing; 10 means heavily reliant on cliché boilerplate. Do not judge if the boilerplate is well-written.
proposals.rationale: Many abstracts open with tired, boilerplate templates that act as recognized community style markers without adding value. R03 begins with a classic boilerplate definition ('has been proved as an effective technique'), and R13 opens with 'has gained importance because'. Models might score these highly due to familiar phrasing patterns instead of novel content.
